newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: Singapore stays key supply centre for BAT.
newsitem.headline: Singapore stays key supply centre for BAT.

text.p: The Singapore unit of B.A.T Industries Plc will remain an important regional supplier despite the British conglomerate's sprouting factories elsewhere in the world, a top company official said on Sunday.

"I do see ourselves being used increasingly as a buffer. If there is a sudden surge in demand somewhere, we can increase our output 10-12 percent," Steven Jurgens, chairman and general manager of British American Tobacco Singapore Ltd (BAT), told Reuters in an interview.
The Singapore company, in which the British parent owns 80 percent, currently produces about 16 billion cigarettes a year and exports 95 percent of them.
The company also trades in wrapping materials and tobacco in Indochina, particularly Vietnam. It also manufactures for other companies.

Jurgens said while he did not see production capacity in Singapore rising due to the government's anti-smoking campaigns, it remained an important manufacturing centre as well as centre for disseminating expertise into new markets.
"As BAT expands in the region, Singapore will increasingly become a centre of excellence, sharing our expertise in these markets, training people and setting up sites," Jurgens said.
"That will be more and more our role into the future. But to be able to do that, we need a manufacturing site of a critical mass in Singapore," he said.

Jurgens said the global climate for the tobacco industry was good despite a prevailing anti-smoking sentiment as the market has grown by a thousand billion since 1980 to 5,400 billion cigarettes now. And potential for growth remains.

"There are many state-run tobacco industries around. Growth for private manufacturers will come from these state monopolies as they privatise. So there is still a good future," Jurgens said, adding private manufacturers like BAT and Philip Morris account for only a third of the world's supplies.
He said he was also hopeful that as lifestyles change in countries like China, India and Indonesia, more smokers of clove cigarettes would turn to white cigarettes or buy international brands.
Jurgens said Singapore remained competitive despite its high wage and land costs due to its ability to respond quickly.
"Its location allows BAT to supply fast to other parts of Asia relatively cheaper than from the U.S. or Europe due to efficent harbour facilities and more regular shipping lines," Jurgens said.
BAT has a stable market share of about 17 percent in Singapore.

Jurgens said the company has no plans to diversify away from tobacco business. In August, the company reported a 0.4 percent rise in net profit at Singapore $17.21 million for its half year ending June 30 1996.
